items.q: A patient with renal failure develops a high phosphate and tingling with carpopedal spasm. Which link explains the neuromuscular features?
items.exp: Hyperphosphatemia may present with hypocalcemic symptoms and vascular medial calcification because phosphate complexes calcium. (Book p889)

items.q: Match the following hyperphosphatemia mechanisms — 1) Phosphate enema 2) CKD 3) Tumor lysis … A) Excess intake B) Reduced excretion C) Intracellular release
items.exp: The page's first three cause groups are increased intake, reduced renal excretion and redistribution from cells to blood. (Book p889)

items.q: The common intake-related trigger singled out for hyperphosphatemia is a phosphate-containing ___.
items.exp: Phosphate-containing enemas can deliver an important phosphate load, especially when renal clearance is impaired. (Book p889)

items.q: After chemotherapy, potassium and phosphate rise while calcium falls. Which process most directly explains the phosphate change?
opts: Increased proximal reabsorption from low FGF23 alone
items.exp: Tumor lysis releases intracellular potassium, phosphate and magnesium; released phosphate complexes calcium. (Book p889)

items.q: Which is the odd one out for the cell-to-blood phosphate redistribution group?
items.exp: Insulin shifts phosphate into cells and can lower serum phosphate. The other options appear in the high-phosphate redistribution group. (Book p889)

items.q: Assess: I Both respiratory and metabolic alkalosis are listed as cell-to-blood phosphate-release causes. II Elevated phosphate necessarily reflects dietary excess.
items.exp: The listed acid-base causes are respiratory or metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis. Renal retention and cellular release also raise phosphate without dietary excess. (Book p889)

items.q: Match the following phosphate-raising settings — 1) Lymphoma 2) Renal failure 3) Massive muscle injury … A) Cellular release B) Increased calcitriol pathway C) Reduced clearance
items.exp: The cause tree places lymphoma with 1α-hydroxylase-associated conditions, renal failure under impaired excretion and rhabdomyolysis under redistribution. (Book p889)

items.q: Which condition is not in the chapter's 1α-hydroxylase-associated hyperphosphatemia group?
items.exp: The source groups acromegaly, lymphoma, sarcoid cells and granulomas with increased calcitriol-related phosphate absorption. Fanconi syndrome instead wastes phosphate. (Book p889)

items.q: A young patient has slowly growing periarticular calcific soft-tissue masses and high phosphate. A recessive FGF23 loss-of-function defect is found. Which diagnosis fits?
items.exp: Loss of FGF23 action impairs phosphate excretion, promoting calcium–phosphate masses in familial tumoral calcinosis. (Book p889)

items.q: The inheritance and FGF23 functional change specified for familial tumoral calcinosis are ___ and ___.
items.exp: The source specifies an autosomal-recessive missense loss-of-function FGF23 variant for this form of tumoral calcinosis. (Book p889)

items.q: Evaluate: I The page names the knee as the common periarticular site of tumoral calcinosis. II The hand radiograph is an example of soft-tissue calcification rather than proof that the hand is the commonest site.
items.exp: The text emphasizes the knee and slow-growing tumor-like soft-tissue masses; the illustration shows calcification in a hand. (Book p889)

items.q: A hyperphosphatemic patient already has high serum calcium. Which listed binder avoids adding a calcium load?
items.exp: The page favors non-calcium phosphate binders, including sevelamer, ferric citrate and sucroferric oxyhydroxide, because calcium-containing binders may worsen hypercalcemia. (Book p889)

items.q: Which is the odd one out among the non-calcium phosphate binders listed?
items.exp: Calcium acetate supplies calcium; the three listed non-calcium alternatives do not. (Book p889)
